final.question: What makes a dashboard something people actually open?
final.form: A dashboard's own anatomy, named chapter by chapter: Title bar, Date range, Filters, Charts, KPI tiles, Annotation, Export
final.object: Eight dashboard tiles, grey and unlit at rest, that rearrange through every chapter and merge into one at the close

swap.reason: The dashboard shell is transferable to any BI analyst, but each chapter is filled by shapes only his confirmed facts produce — a line from five hours to two, Lisbon's parishes, twelve dots gathering, a still notebook page — and the through-line is his own sentence about dashboards people actually use.

backdrop.reason: The tiles are the carriers of the content — the numbers and charts sit on their faces — and the argument is made by their rearrangement from unlit grid to timeline to charts to KPIs to one merged tile, so deleting the object would delete the page's evidence, not its decoration.

depth.reason: The chapters follow a dashboard's life in a fixed order — loading, filtering, charting, totalling, annotating, exporting — with the question posed on the first screen and answered on the last, so the sequence cannot be shuffled.

clipart.reason: The central object is a BI tile grid that expands into charts and flips to oversized KPI numbers — the stock emblem of analytics work, with the hackathon tile rendered literally as a bar chart.

honesty.reason: Every contested figure and title is corrected to what is true, 35% is dropped, the paper and the hackathon team are handled accurately and Meridian is capped at its one public figure; the single overreach is the caption claiming all six tools on all eight items.

thirty_seconds.reason: The first screen carries his name, role, tagline and one proof (the Meridian tile resolving to "200+ staff") before any scrolling, and the nav rail has a "get in touch" link jumping straight to his email and CV.

plain_reader.reason: "I make dashboards people actually use" and "What makes a dashboard something people actually open?" are his own plain words, free of jargon and pointed enough that a hiring analyst would take them seriously.

judgement.summary: A scroll-driven page built as a working dashboard: eight tiles, one per confirmed thing Rafael has done, that load as an unlit grid, line up into a timeline, expand into charts drawn from his real numbers, flip to KPIs, take Beatriz's quote as a pinned annotation, and merge into a single contact tile that answers the question posed at the top. Its greatest weakness is that the central object is the emblem of the job it describes — a BI tile grid of charts and KPI numbers is the most predictable possible form for an analyst's site, and its most distinctive beats (the 5-to-2-hour line, the twelve dots) have to carry all the particularity the shell lacks.
